The position of an element in the sorted array is its rank; write that rank back to the\n     output vector at the stored original index.\n\nHPX already provides parallel versions of the STL algorithms.  \nWe use  \n\n* `hpx::parallel::stable_sort` – parallel stable sort, executed with the `par` execution policy.  \n* A tiny sequential loop to write the ranks back (the work is O(N) and far cheaper than the sort,\n  so the extra parallelism would not give a measurable benefit).\n\nAll work is done inside the single `ranks` function – no helper functions are introduced.\n\n```cpp\n#include <vector>\n#include <utility>          // std::pair\n#include <cstddef>          // std::size_t\n\n// HPX parallel algorithm facilities\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithm.hpp>\n#include <hpx/execution.hpp>\n\n/*  Compute the rank of each element in `x`.\n    The rank is the index the element would have after a **stable**\n    ascending sort of the whole vector.\n    The result is stored in `ranks` (must be resized by the function).\n\n    Example\n        x = [3.1, 2.8, 9.1, 0.4, 3.14]\n        ranks = [2, 1, 4, 0, 3]\n\n    The implementation uses HPX's parallel stable_sort for maximum\n    performance on multi‑core / many‑core systems.\n*/\nvoid ranks(std::vector<float> const& x, std::vector<std::size_t>& ranks)\n{\n    const std::size_t n = x.size();\n    ranks.resize(n);\n\n    // 1) Build an auxiliary array of (value, original_index)\n    std::vector<std::pair<float, std::size_t>> aux;\n    aux.reserve(n);\n    for (std::size_t i = 0;                     // make sure the output vector is large enough\n\n    using pair_t = std::pair<float, std::size_t>;\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 1) Build a temporary vector of (value, original_index) pairs.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<pair_t> tmp;\n    tmp.reserve(n);\n    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i)\n        tmp.emplace_back(x[i], i);\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 2) Stable‑sort the pairs in parallel.\n    //    The comparator first compares the value, then the original index\n    //    to guarantee stability (earlier duplicate gets the lower rank).\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    hpx::parallel::stable_sort(\n        hpx::parallel::execution::par,          // parallel execution policy\n        tmp.begin(),\n        tmp.end(),\n        [](pair_t const& a, pair_t const& b) -> bool\n        {\n            if (a.first < b.first)  return true;\n            if (a.first > b.first)  return false;\n            return a.second < b.second; the `par` execution policy lets HPX split the work automatically. |\n| 3️⃣   | Write the rank (`sorted_position`) back to the user‑provided `ranks` vector. | A parallel `for_loop` avoids a single‑thread bottleneck for very large inputs. |\n| 4️⃣   | All allocations are done once, no helper functions are introduced. | Keeps the code compact and cache‑friendly. |\n\nBelow is a self‑contained implementation that follows the specification\nexactly – it works for empty inputs, handles duplicates correctly, and\nuses only HPX parallel primitives.\n\n```cpp\n#include <vector>\n#include <utility>          // std::pair\n#include <cstddef>          // std::size_t\n\n// HPX parallel algorithms\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithm.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/for_loop.hpp>\n#include <hpx/execution.hpp>\n\n/*  For each value in the vector `x` compute its index in the *stable* sorted\n    vector and store the result in `ranks`.\n\n    Example\n        x = [3.1, 2.8, 9.1, 0.4, 3.14]   → ranks = [2, 1, 4, 0, 3]\n\n    The function assumes that HPX has already been initialized (e.g. via\n    `hpx_main` or `hpx::init`).  No helper functions are used – everything\n    lives inside this single function.\n*/\nvoid ranks(std::vector<float> const& x, std::vector<std::size_t>& ranks)\n{\n    const std::size_t n = x.size();\n\n    // --------------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 1) Prepare (value, original_index) pairs.\n    // --------------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<std::pair<float, std::size_t>> tmp;\n    tmp.reserve(n);\n    for (std::size_t i = 0; Build a temporary array that stores both the value and its original index  \n   `tmp[i] = { x[i], i }`.\n2. **Stable‑sort** this array by the value (and by the original index as a tie‑breaker – this makes the sort stable even if the algorithm itself is not).\n3. After sorting, the element that ends up at position `k` originally came from index `tmp[k].second`.  \n   Therefore `rank[ tmp[k].second ] = k`.\n\nAll three steps can be expressed with HPX parallel algorithms:\n\n* `hpx::parallel::stable_sort` – parallel stable sort.\n* `hpx::parallel::for_loop` – parallel assignment of the final ranks.\n\nThe implementation below follows these steps, uses only the standard library and HPX, and does **not** rely on any helper functions.\n\n```cpp\n#include <hpx/hpx_main.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithm.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/execution.hpp>\n\n#include <vector>\n#include <utility>   // std::pair\n#include <cstddef>   // std::size_t\n\n/*  Compute the rank of each element in `x`.\n    The rank is the index of the element in a *stable* sorted copy of `x`.\n    The result is written into `ranks` (which is resized to match `x`).\n\n    Example\n        x = [3.1, 2.8, 9.1, 0.4, 3.14]\n        ranks = [2, 1, 4, 0, 3]\n\n    The implementation uses HPX parallel algorithms and contains no\n    auxiliary helper functions.\n*/\nvoid ranks(std::vector<float> const& x, std::vector<std::size_t>& ranks)\n{\n    using hpx::parallel::execution::par;\n    using hpx::parallel::stable_sort;\n    using hpx::parallel::for_loop;\n\n    const std::size_t n = x.size();\n    ranks.resize(n);\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 1) Build a temporary array of (value, original_index) pairs.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<std::pair<float, std::size_t>> tmp;\n    tmp.reserve(n);\n    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i)\n        tmp.emplace_back(x[i], i);\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 2) Parallel stable sort by value.\n    //    The comparator also uses the original index as a tie‑breaker,\n    //    guaranteeing stability even if the underlying algorithm is not.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    stable_sort(par,\n                tmp.begin(), tmp.end(),\n                [](const std::pair<float, std::size_t>& a,\n                   const std::pair<float, std::size_t>& b) {\n                    if (a.first < b.first)  return true;\n                    if (a.first > b.first)  return false;\n                    // equal values – keep original order\n                    return a.second < b.second;\n                });\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 3) Write the ranks back to the output vector in parallel.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    for_loop(par, std::size_t(0), n,\n             [&](std::size_t k) {\n                 // element that ended up at position k Pair every value with its original index: `(value, index)`.\n2. Stable‑sort the pairs by `value`.  \n   Because the sort is *stable*, equal values stay in the order of their original indices, which gives the required ranking for duplicates.\n3. Walk through the sorted pairs; the current position `i` is the rank of the element whose original index is stored in the pair.\n\nAll three steps can be expressed with HPX parallel algorithms:\n\n* `hpx::parallel::stable_sort` – parallel stable sort.\n* `hpx::parallel::for_loop` – parallel assignment of the ranks.\n* The construction of the temporary vector of pairs is cheap and done sequentially (it is only `O(N)` and does not dominate the overall cost).\n\nThe implementation below follows the “no helper functions” rule – everything is written directly inside `ranks`.\n\n```cpp\n#include <hpx/hpx_main.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithm.hpp>\n#include <hpx/execution.hpp>\n\n#include <vector>\n#include <utility>   // std::pair\n#include <cstddef>   // std::size_t\n\n/*  For each value in the vector x compute its index in the sorted vector.\n    Store the results in `ranks`.\n    Use HPX to compute in parallel.  Assume HPX has already been initialized.\n\n    Example:\n        input : [3.1, 2.8, 9.1, 0.4, 3.14]\n        output: [2, 1, 4, 0, 3]\n\n        input : [100, 7.6, 16.1, 18, 7.6]\n        output: [4, 0, 1, 2, 3]\n*/\nvoid ranks(std::vector<float> const& x, std::vector<std::size_t>& ranks)\n{\n    const std::size_t n = x.size();\n\n    // Resize the output vector once – no re‑allocations later.\n    ranks.resize(n);\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 1) Build (value, original_index) pairs.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<std::pair<float, std::size_t>> tmp;\n    tmp.reserve(n);\n    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i)\n        tmp.emplace_back(x[i], i);\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 2) Stable‑sort the pairs by the value.\n    //    `hpx::execution::par` enables parallel execution.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    hpx::parallel::stable_sort(\n        hpx::execution::par,\n        tmp.begin(),\n        tmp.end(),\n        [](const std::pair<float, std::size_t>& a,\n           const std::pair<float, std::size_t>& b) {\n            return a.first < b.first; original_index) pairs.\n    // ----------------------------------------------------------------------\n    using pair_t = std::pair<float, std::size_t>;\n    std::vector<pair_t> tmp;\n    tmp.reserve(n);\n    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i)\n        tmp.emplace_back(x[i], i);\n\n    // ----------------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 2) Parallel stable Build a temporary array that stores both the value and its original index.  \n2. **Stable‑sort** that array by the value (so equal values keep their original order).  \n3. Write the rank (`position in the sorted array`) back to the output vector at the stored original index.\n\nAll three steps can be expressed with HPX parallel algorithms:\n\n* `hpx::parallel::stable_sort` – parallel stable sort.  \n* `hpx::parallel::for_loop` – parallel fill‑in of the result vector.  \n\nNo helper functions are used; everything lives inside `ranks()`.\n\n```cpp\n#include <vector>\n#include <utility>          // std::pair\n#include <cstddef>          // std::size_t\n\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithm.hpp>   // stable_sort, for_loop\n#include <hpx/execution.hpp>            // execution policies\n\n/*  For each value in the vector `x` compute its index in the *stable* sorted\n    vector and store the result in `ranks`.\n\n    Example\n        x = [3.1, 2.8, 9.1, 0.4, 3.14]   →   ranks = [2, 1, 4, 0, 3]\n\n    The function assumes that HPX has already been initialized (e.g. via\n    `hpx_main` or `hpx::init`).  It is completely thread‑safe and makes full\n    use of HPX’s parallel execution policies.\n*/\nvoid ranks(std::vector<float> const& x, std::vector<std::size_t>& ranks)\n{\n    const std::size_t n = x.size();\n\n    // --------------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 1) Build (value, original_index) pairs.\n    // --------------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<std::pair<float, std::size_t>> tmp;\n    tmp.reserve(n);\n    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i)\n        tmp.emplace_back(x[i], i);\n\n    // --------------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 2) Stable‑sort the pairs by the value.\n    //    `hpx::execution::par` selects a parallel execution policy.\n    // --------------------------------------------------------------------\n    hpx::parallel::stable_sort(\n        hpx::execution::par,\n        tmp.begin(),\n        tmp.end(),\n        [](const std::pair<float, std::size_t>& a,\n           const std::pair<float, std::size_t>& b)\n        {\n            return a.first < b.first;          // compare only the values\n        });\n\n    // --------------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 3) Write the rank (the position in the sorted array) back to the\n    //    output vector at the original index.\n    // --------------------------------------------------------------------\n    ranks.resize(n);                         // make sure the output is sized\n\n    hpx::parallel::for_loop(\n        hpx::execution::par,\n        std::size_t(0),\n        n,\n        [&](std::size_t sorted_pos)\n        {\n            const std::size_t original_idx = tmp[sorted_pos].second;\n            ranks[original_idx] = sorted_pos; // rank == sorted position\n        });\n}\n```\n\n### Why this is fast\n\n* **Parallel stable sort** – HPX’s `stable_sort` internally partitions the data and merges sorted sub‑ranges in parallel, giving near‑linear speed‑up on many cores while preserving the order of equal elements (required by the examples).\n* **Parallel rank write‑back** – The final `for_loop` distributes the `n` assignments across the available threads, eliminating any serial bottleneck.\n* **Cache‑friendly layout** – The temporary vector of `std::pair<float,size_t>` is contiguous, so the sort works on a single memory block, minimizing cache misses.\n\nThe implementation is self‑contained, uses only standard‑library types plus HPX parallel primitives, and respects the “no helper functions” constraint.", 'source_write_success': True, 'did_build': False, 'build_exit_code': 1, 'build_stdout': '', 'build_stderr': "In file included from cpp/benchmarks/sort/42_sort_sorted_ranks/hpx.cc:21:\n/tmp/tmpeld6ep14/generated-code.hpp:1:287: error: missing terminating ' character\n    1 | analysisWe need to write code using HPX to compute ranks (index in sorted order) for each element. Build (value, original_index) pairs.\n       ------------------------------------------------------------------ */\n    std::vector<std::pair<float, std::size_t>> tmp;\n    tmp.reserve(n);\n    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < n; ++i)\n        tmp.emplace_back(x[i], i);\n\n    /* ------------------------------------------------------------------\n       2. Stable‑sort the pairs in parallel.\n       ------------------------------------------------------------------ */\n    hpx::parallel::stable_sort(\n        hpx::parallel::execution::par,          // parallel execution policy\n        tmp.begin(),\n        tmp.end(),\n        // comparator: first by value, then by original index (guarantees stability)\n        [](const std::pair<float, std::size_t>& a,\n           const std::pair<float, std::size_t>& b) noexcept\n        {\n            if (a.first < b.first)  return true;\n            if (a.first > b.first)  return false;\n            return a.second < b.second;   // tie‑break on original position\n        });\n\n    /* ------------------------------------------------------------------\n       3. Write the rank (sorted position) back to the output vector.\n       ------------------------------------------------------------------ */\n    hpx::parallel::for_loop(\n        hpx::parallel::execution::par,          // parallel execution policy\n        std::size_t(0), n,\n        [&](std::size_t i)                     // i is the position in the sorted array\n        {\n            const std::size_t orig_idx = tmp[i].second;\n            ranks[orig_idx] = i;               // i is exactly the rank of that element\n        });\n}\n```\n\n--------------------------------------------------------------------\n\n### Why this is fast\n\n| Step | HPX primitive | Reason for performance |\n|------|----------------|------------------------|\n| Build pairs | plain sequential loop (tiny work, negligible overhead) | Memory is allocated once (`reserve`) and cache‑friendly. |\n| Stable sort | `hpx::parallel::stable_sort` with `par` policy | HPX splits the range, sorts sub‑ranges concurrently, then merges – fully exploiting all cores while preserving stability. |\n| Write ranks | `hpx::parallel::for_loop` with `par` policy | Independent writes to distinct indices; HPX schedules the iterations across threads with work‑stealing, giving excellent load balance. |\n\nAll three phases are *embarrassingly parallel* (no inter‑iteration dependencies), so the implementation scales almost linearly with the number of hardware threads.\n\n--------------------------------------------------------------------\n\n### Correctness notes\n\n* The comparator first orders by the floating‑point value and, **only when the values are equal**, by the original index.  \n  This reproduces the behaviour of a stable sort and matches the required output for duplicate values.\n* The final loop stores `i` (the element’s position in the sorted array) into `ranks[original_index]`.  \n  By definition this is the rank of the original element.\n* The function resizes `ranks` to the correct length, making it safe to call with an empty output vector.\n\n--------------------------------------------------------------------\n\n### Usage example\n\n```cpp\n#include <iostream>\n\nint main()\n{\n    std::vector<float> data = {100, 7.6f, 16.1f, 18, 7.6f};\n    std::vector<std::size_t> r;\n\n    ranks(data, r);\n\n    for (auto v : r) std::cout << v << ' ';\n    // prints: 4 0 1 2 3\n}\n```\n\nThe program runs entirely on HPX’s default thread pool; Zero‑valued elements stay exactly where they were.\n    The heavy work (the actual sort) is performed with HPX’s parallel\n    algorithms.\n\n    Example\n        input : [8, 4, 0, 9, 8, 0, 1, -1, 7]\n        output: [-1, 1, 0, 4, 7, 0, 8, 8, 9]\n*/\nvoid sortIgnoreZero(std::vector<int> &x)\n{\n    using namespace hpx::parallel::execution;   // par, par_unseq, …\n    using hpx::parallel::sort;\n    using hpx::parallel::for_loop;\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 1) Gather the indices of all non‑zero elements.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<std::size_t> idx;\n    idx.reserve(x.size());\n\n    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i)\n        if (x[i] != 0)\n            idx.push_back(i);\n\n    // Nothing to do if there are 0 or 1 non‑zero elements.\n    if (idx.size() <= 1)\n        return;\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 2) Copy the non‑zero values to a temporary buffer.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<int> values;\n    values.reserve(idx.size());\n\n    for (std::size_t i : idx)\n        values.push_back(x[i]);\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 3) Sort the temporary buffer **in parallel**.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    sort(par, values.begin(), values.end());\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 4) Write the sorted values back to the original vector.\n    //    The write‑back itself is parallelised.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    for_loop(par, std::size_t(0), idx.size(),\n        [&](std::size_t k)\n        {\n            x[idx[k]] = values[k];\n        });\n}\n```\n\n### Why this is efficient\n\n* **Parallel sort** – `hpx::parallel::sort(par, …)` distributes the work over all HPX worker threads, giving you true multi‑core speed‑up for the expensive comparison‑based sorting phase.\n* **Cache‑friendly** – only the non‑zero elements are moved into a compact temporary buffer, so the sort works on a dense array          // parallel execution policy\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 1) Gather all non‑zero values (parallel copy_if)\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<int> nonzeros;\n    nonzeros.reserve(x.size());          // avoid reallocations\n\n    hpx::parallel::copy_if(\n        par,                            // execution policy\n        x.begin(), x.end(),            // source range\n        std::back_inserter(nonzeros),  // destination\n        [](int v) { return v != 0; snippet.\n\nassistantfinal**Solution Overview**\n\nWe have to sort the *non‑zero* elements of a `std::vector<int>` while leaving every `0` exactly where it originally was.  \nThe algorithm is:\n\n1. **Collect the positions of the non‑zero elements** – this is a small auxiliary vector of indices.  \n2. **Gather the values at those positions** into a second auxiliary vector.  \n3. **Sort the values in parallel** with HPX’s `hpx::parallel::sort`.  \n4. **Scatter the sorted values back** to the original positions – this can also be done with a parallel loop because each index is written exactly once.\n\nAll work is performed inside a single function, no helper functions are introduced, and the implementation uses only HPX parallel algorithms (`par` execution policy) to obtain high performance on multi‑core systems.\n\n```cpp\n#include <vector>\n#include <cstddef>\n\n#include <hpx/hpx_main.hpp>\n#include <hpx/execution.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithms/sort.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithms/for_loop.hpp>\n\n/*  Sort the vector x in ascending order ignoring elements with value 0.\n    Zero‑valued elements stay at their original positions.\n    The sorting of the non‑zero elements is performed in parallel with HPX.\n\n    Example\n        input : [8, 4, 0, 9, 8, 0, 1, -1, 7]\n        output: [-1, 1, 0, 4, 7, 0, 8, 8, 9]\n*/\nvoid sortIgnoreZero(std::vector<int> &x)\n{\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 1) Find the indices of all non‑zero entries.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<std::size_t> nz_idx;\n    nz_idx.reserve(x.size());\n\n    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i)\n        if (x[i] != 0)\n            nz_idx.push_back(i);\n\n    // Nothing to do if the vector is empty or contains only zeros.\n    if (nz_idx.empty())\n        return;\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 2) Gather the corresponding values.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<int> nz_vals;\n    nz_vals.reserve(nz_idx.size());\n\n    for (std::size_t i : nz_idx)\n        nz_vals.push_back(x[i]);\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 3) Sort the non‑zero values in parallel.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // Use the parallel execution policy provided by HPX.\n    hpx::parallel::sort(hpx::execution::par, nz_vals.begin(), nz_vals.end());\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 4) Scatter the sorted values back to their original positions.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // Each iteration writes to a distinct location, therefore a parallel\n    // for‑loop is safe.\n    hpx::parallel::for_loop(\n **Data‑locality** – The auxiliary vectors contain only the elements that actually need work, so the amount of memory moved is minimal.\n* **Parallel sort** – `hpx::parallel::sort` distributes the work across all available cores, giving the same asymptotic complexity as a sequential sort (`O(m log m)`, where *m* is the number of non‑zero elements) but with a much smaller wall‑clock time on order ignoring elements with value 0.\n    Zero‑valued elements stay exactly where they were.\n    The non‑zero part is sorted in parallel using HPX.\n\n    Example\n        input : [8, 4, 0, 9, 8, 0,               // positions of non‑zero values\n    idx.reserve(x.size());\n\n    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < x.size(); ++i)\n        if (x[i] != 0)\n            idx.push_back(i);\n\n    // Nothing to do if there are 0 or 1 non‑zero elements.\n    if (idx.size() <= 1)\n        return;\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 2) Gather the non‑zero values.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::vector<int> vals;                      // the values that will be sorted\n    vals.reserve(idx.size());\n\n    for (std::size_t i : idx)\n        vals.push_back(x[i]);\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 3) Sort the values in parallel.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    hpx::parallel::sort(par, vals.begin(), vals.end());\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 4) Scatter the sorted values back to their original positions.\n    //    Each iteration works on a distinct index → no data race.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    hpx::parallel::for_loop(\n        par,\n        std::size_t(0),\n        idx.size(),\n        [&](std::size_t k) { x[idx[k]] = vals[k]; every element that is equal to `0` at its original position**.  \nThe algorithm must be parallelised with HPX, but we are not allowed to introduce helper functions – everything has to live inside `sortIgnoreZero`.\n\nThe most straight‑forward way to achieve the required behaviour is:\n\n1. **Collect** all non‑zero values into a temporary buffer.  \n2. **Sort** that buffer with HPX’s parallel `sort`.  \n3. **Scatter** the sorted values back to the original vector, writing only into the positions that originally contained a non‑zero element.\n\nAll three steps can be expressed with HPX parallel algorithms (`count`, `for_each`, `sort`).  \nThe only synchronisation needed is an atomic counter that gives each thread a unique index into the temporary buffer.\n\nBelow is a self‑contained, high‑performance implementation that follows the rules above.\n\n```cpp\n#include <hpx/hpx_main.hpp>\n#include <hpx/execution.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithms/count.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithms/for_each.hpp>\n#include <hpx/parallel/algorithms/sort.hpp>\n\n#include <vector>\n#include <atomic>\n\n/*  Sort the vector x in ascending order ignoring elements with value 0.\n    Zero‑valued elements stay at their original indices.\n    The work is performed with HPX parallel algorithms.\n    Example:\n        input : [8, 4, 0, 9, 8, 0, 1, -1, 7]\n        output: [-1, 1, 0, 4, 7, 0, 8, 8, 9]\n*/\nvoid sortIgnoreZero(std::vector<int> &x)\n{\n    using namespace hpx::execution;          // par, unseq, etc.\n    using hpx::parallel::count;\n    using hpx::parallel::for_each;\n    using hpx::parallel::sort;\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 1) Determine how many non‑zero elements we have.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::size_t nz_cnt = count(par, x.begin(), x.end(),\n                               [](int v) { return v != 0; });\n\n    // Allocate a contiguous buffer that will hold *only* the non‑zero values.\n    std::vector<int> nz;\n    nz.resize(nz_cnt);\n\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    // 2) Fill the buffer in parallel.\n    // -----------------------------------------------------------------\n    std::atomic<std::size_t> fill_idx{0};\n\n    for_each(par, x.begin(), x.end(),\n             [&](int v)\n             {\n                 if (v != 0)\n                 {\n                     // each
